comments.author: dizzant
comments.text:
I'm surprised that 10 years later, the article still teaches an incorrect conceptual understanding of "quantization".
The context heavily implies that quantization is "discarding information" generally (e.g. clipping, masking). The wikipedia article he links in the footnote disagrees, and so do I:
> quantization is the process of mapping input values from a large set (often a continuous set) to output values in a (countable) smaller set, often with a finite number of elements.
Quantization is a function over values, or the image itself. Clipping and masking, by contrast, are functions over the space/frequency dimensions, i.e. the pixel indices ("preimage"). A rule like "apply a circular mask" or "drop the first quadrant" does not depend on the values!
The most extreme example of quantization is a threshold filter. Regardless of location, output "1" if the pixel is brighter than X, or "0" otherwise. This depends only on the value, not on the location. He also misses the opportunity to point out that chroma subsampling is another application of quantization, this time to chroma values (drop the low-order bits).

comments.text: The rebuild-instead-of-editing-in-place choice is the part that would make me trust this with a real file. Most in-browser editors that patch bytes in place scare me because a single bad page write can corrupt the b-tree, and you only find out later. Rebuilding the file and then running PRAGMA integrity_check on the output is a much stronger story, even if it explains why indexes, views and triggers are left as a recreate script rather than preserved. comments.author: icecheese
comments.text:
ANSI art is still alive. We have some great modern editors, like Moebius, Durdraw, Icydraw and Pablodraw.
Some of them, like Durdraw, have fully embraced the extended Unicode character set (Utf-8 encoding instead of IBM's Code Page 437) and extended colors (xterm 256 colors instead of the traditional 16 colors), keeping ANSI art relevant and viable into the foreseeable future.
People are making logos and assets for their modern TUI apps and games, for example. Neovim themes. Ly display manager wallpapers.
I am personally glad to see that the medium is coming back into relevance. It was such a fun part of digital culture and creativity in the 90s. I hope the next generation gets to experience some of that thanks to modern tooling, instead of just observed as a relic of the past.
Edit: There is also a debate as to whether Unicode/Utf-8 characters with ANSI and Xterm escape codes constitutes "ANSI art." Some are calling it "UNSI art," or just modern terminal art.
Also, shout-out to the CP437 ANSI artists who continue to evolve the artistic styles of the medium, push the envelope, and release new ANSI packs. Hard, valuable work.

comments.author: lazystone
comments.text:
> In theory, the whole AOT cache idea sounds like something that should only affect the class data and not perform any native compilation
https://openjdk.org/jeps/544
> Non-Goals
> It is not a goal to support cross-compilation. Code compiled in a training run must run on the same CPU architecture, with the same set of features, in subsequent production runs.

comments.author: pron
comments.text:
For the past several years, Java features are released piecemeal, with each piece released as soon as it can be useful to some significant portion of users or users who can offer useful feedback (and when it's not expected to restrict future pieces). The AOT cache is already used in production despite not being as user-friendly as it could be, because the companies using it find it valuable.
The first use case is the very common one (for Java) where developers control deployment (internal deployment). The last
basic
building block, caching machine code, will be released next year in JDK 28, and then the feature is likely to evolve to better support other use cases, such as external deployment.

comments.author: deepsun
comments.text:
> What would be needed is some sort of compatibility switch that disables all optional CPU features. Sure, you will get some reduced performance of the compiled code, but in exchange, a faster startup time.
I think other AOT-compiled languages don't opt in for the lowest set of CPU features -- they just detect them at runtime and use whenever present, all in compiled machine code.

comments.author: pjmlp
comments.text:

There are plenty of other AOT/JIT cache approaches in the Java ecosystem already, with more mature deployment experience of several years, namely:

Technology based on process snapshots CRaC for Amazon OpenJDK distro (Correcto), and OpenJ9, is also another approach available for some time.
